text: Every line an AI agent writes stands on someone else's work.
But an AI agent is the first user of open source that knows exactly who it owes.
You can still choose not to pay. You just can't say you didn't know.
Open source is worth an estimated eight point eight trillion dollars to the companies that use it. Rewriting it once would cost about four billion.
Five percent of developers, roughly three thousand people, create ninety-six percent of that value.
When Heartbleed hit, OpenSSL ran on under two thousand dollars a year. The xz backdoor was planted over two years, in a project run by one unpaid maintainer.
Now AI writes the code, and fewer people ever see the docs or the sponsor button. Tailwind lost about forty percent of its docs traffic, and nearly eighty percent of its revenue.

Why PayPal? Maintainers live everywhere. PayPal Payouts reach ninety-six markets in twenty-four currencies, with just an email address. A subscription holds the human's mandate, and one batch pays everyone, once.
Setup is two steps. Set a monthly budget, and one click redirects to PayPal to approve it. That approval is the agent's mandate, and its ceiling.
Then one hook line. Package names and depth only. Never source code.
At month end, the AI Treasurer answers typed questions: how critical is each package, and how much do its maintainers need? Code turns those answers into amounts.
Same budget. Judgment moves this package from sixty-nine dollars to one sixty-one.
A security advisory? The AI can propose a grant. Only a human can approve it, on PayPal.
Month end. A poisoned README asks for the maximum score. The answer is rejected, and a neutral weight is used.
A recipient who just changed their payout email is held.
Seven invariants, checked in code, before a cent moves.
The AI decides where the money goes. The code decides where it can never go.
Maya, a fictional maintainer, sees every payment, and exactly why.
Run it twice. Same batch. No double pay.
And both sides get a statement anyone can recompute.
